title: ASIC slams private credit fund conflicts after probe
full_text:
The corporate regulator has slammed the practices of funds operating in Australia's $250 billion private credit sector, saying that they are too opaque and complicated, as it confirmed a probe into the activities of the Bathla Group.
In a scathing 58-page report to be released on Tuesday, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission said one fund was banking secret payments four times larger than its disclosed management fee, while some financial advisers were telling clients to pour up to 87 per cent of their money into private credit funds.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said private credit funds were still leaving their investors in the dark about how their funds were being invested, how they were being charged, and where their funds were being directed, following the regulator's second major investigation into private credit in the past 18 months.
"Investors should not need a PhD in corporate finance to understand how funds operate," she said.
The regulator used compulsory powers to assess the operations of 24 wholesale and retail private credit funds with $18 billion of assets under management, and extended that to a sample of advice provided by financial planners.
The probe found that nine of out 12 retail private credit funds reviewed did not disclose key investment information, while 10 out of 12 funds had poorly designed disclosures about the suitability of their products. It also uncovered complex and opaque fund structures and related-party transactions, which were not always disclosed to investors.
ASIC highlighted one case where about 17 per cent of a fund's assets were transferred to related funds managed by the same group in a single year.
The report comes after a strong period of growth in the popularity of private credit funds, which were pitched to investors as offering high and reliable interest rates without the volatility of shares.
That has since soured as more funds with exposure to real estate construction are dealing with defaults and elevated redemption requests as interest rates increase and property prices fall.
The August collapse of western Sydney-based developer Bathla Group, which borrowed over $3.3 billion from private credit funds, sent shockwaves through the industry and forced the likes of Centuria Bass Credit and CVS Lane Capital Partners to suspend withdrawals from their funds.
Constant confirmed that the regulator had "commenced a formal investigation in relation to the conduct of the affairs of the Bathla Group", and was also making inquiries in relation to private lenders.
However, the sector's woes are not limited to Bathla lenders, as fund managers such as Merricks Capital, MA Financial Group, and Metrics Credit Partners have been forced to impose temporary freezes on withdrawals.
Constant said the private credit industry had a lot of work to do to lift its game, particularly as the economy slowed, and loan losses were expected to rise.
"This is our line in the sand about managing these interests, these relationships, and moving to more transparency, tighter governance, and appropriate conflicts of interest practices to support those structures and the fair treatment of investors."
Among the corporate regulator's key concerns was that private credit funds were making substantially more money from their lending activities than they were charging underlying investors via management fees.
This occurs via so-called upfront or arranger fees, in which the borrower pays the fund manager directly for setting up the loan, and via retaining a portion of interest payments.
ASIC said just two out of the 22 funds that responded "passed on the full economic benefit of interest and borrower fees onto investors" while retail private credit funds retained as much as 5.6 per cent in interest margins relative to what was paid out to investors. ASIC also found that more than half of the wholesale and retail funds surveyed did not pass on default interest charged to borrowers to their investors.
Constant said she was not surprised by the gap between fees and interest charged to borrowers and the returns remitted to investors in the fund.
The report said the lack of disclosure made it hard for investors to determine if they were being appropriately rewarded for risking their capital. "We are not the returns police. We are not the margin police. However, we are the conduct regulator, and we are calling out that the pricing of risk and the treatment of risk need to be consistent with what's disclosed to those investors," she said.
In the lead-up to the report, ASIC placed temporary stop orders on six fixed-income funds after identifying problems with disclosures relating to their appropriateness for investors, or target market determinations. These prevent funds from raising further funds until issues are addressed.
On Monday, ASIC took action against Angas Securities, which did not adequately disclose exposure to failed property lender Bathla to unitholders in one of its funds.
Nine Entertainment Co.
